title: Gastroesophageal Junction and Pylorus Distensibility Before and After Sleeve Gastrectomy—pilot Study with EndoFlipTM

sections.title: The Reflux Problem After Sleeve Gastrectomy
sections.markdown: Sleeve gastrectomy, one of the most common weight-loss operations, has a well-known downside: many patients develop acid reflux afterward, or see existing reflux get worse. Surgeons still can't reliably predict who that will happen to. This pilot study asked whether a device called the **EndoFlip**, a balloon-tipped probe that measures how easily a muscular valve stretches open, could give an early warning.

sections.title: What Distensibility Measures
sections.markdown: The key measurement is the **distensibility index (DI)**, essentially how floppy a sphincter is. A higher number means the valve opens more readily under pressure, which for the **gastroesophageal junction (GEJ)**, the muscular gate between esophagus and stomach, means stomach acid can escape upward more easily. The team also measured the **pylorus**, the valve at the stomach's exit.

sections.title: How the Study Was Run
sections.markdown: Nine patients at a Swiss university hospital were tested before surgery, during surgery, and again a year later, using endoscopy, pH-impedance monitoring (the standard test for acid exposure), manometry, and the EndoFlip. Reflux was classified by the Lyon Consensus definition: acid exposure time above 6 percent and more than 80 reflux episodes.

sections.title: Key Results and Findings
sections.markdown:
Two findings stand out. Both valves loosened after surgery: GEJ distensibility roughly doubled (1.4 to 2.9 square millimeters per millimeter of mercury, p = 0.046), and pyloric distensibility also rose significantly (6.0 to 13.1, p = 0.046). The looser pylorus may explain faster stomach emptying after sleeve gastrectomy, which contradicts an earlier report by Desprez and colleagues.

More interesting for prediction: patients who had reflux a year after surgery already had a significantly looser GEJ *before* the operation (2.6 versus 0.5, p = 0.031). Weight loss at one year did not differ between the reflux and no-reflux groups, so the valve measurement, not the amount of weight lost, tracked with reflux.

sections.title: Limitations and What Comes Next
sections.markdown: With only nine patients, this is a signal rather than a conclusion. The authors note that reference values for normal distensibility don't yet exist, and larger studies are needed before the measurement can guide surgical decisions.
